title: US Air Force says it responded to 'suspected drones' over RAF Lakenheath
description: The US Air Force said it responded to "suspected unauthorised drone activity" over RAF Lakenheath in Suffolk on Friday evening.No personnel, aircraft
body: The US Air Force said it responded to "suspected unauthorised drone activity" over RAF Lakenheath in Suffolk on Friday evening.No personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected, a spokesperson for the US Air Force said.It comes after unconfirmed reports that sirens were sounded at the base, which residents reported hearing from a nearby village. The Ministry of Defence has been contacted for comment.West Suffolk MP Nick Timothy said he had been in touch with authorities at the base, and was told "there is no threat to the public, and the incident is now resolved"."Given the raised threat level, I continue to encourage everyone to report anything suspicious or out of the ordinary to the authorities," he added in a social media post.Earlier this week, at least 12 US Air Force aircraft departed the nearby RAF Mildenhall base.They included two Boeing Stratotanker KC-135 refuelling aircraft, with one apparently headed towards Germany and another seen landing at Prestwick Airport near Glasgow.

schema.headline: US Air Force says it responded to 'suspected drones' over RAF Lakenheath

title: Reform and Tory spokesmen in angry clash over immigration at Piddington
description: A press conference led by Piddington Parish Council chairman Tim McNally took place on Friday after Housing Secretary Angela Rayner approved the Home
body: A press conference led by Piddington Parish Council chairman Tim McNally took place on Friday after Housing Secretary Angela Rayner approved the Home Office's application to change the use of the site for asylum accommodation.The Home Office said this would allow it to continue developing the plan but that no final decision on the site had been taken.There has been significant local opposition to the proposal and a legal challenge to the planning decision is expected from the parish council.In September, Piddington symbolically voted to leave the UK over the planned use for the site in Oxfordshire. Politicians from the Conservatives and Reform have made several visits to Piddington, a village of about 350 people, to show their support for campaigners.Speaking on Friday, Philp said a future Conservative government would shut the asylum accommodation "straight away" if it was opened by Labour.Yusuf made clear Reform's opposition to the plans before his focus switched to the Conservatives.He said: "It's obviously true that we would not be gathered here today and 1,200 men would not be being dumped into this beautiful village were it not for the actions of the Conservative government."So I actually want to ask you Chris, would you actually like to apologise for the things you did in government to bring hundreds of thousands of people into this country illegally?"Philp, a former immigration minister, described Yusuf's remarks as "disingenuous" and argued the migrants who could be housed near Piddington will have arrived in the country while Labour has been in power.He said the Conservatives are under new leadership and he hoped the politicians could "stand in solidarity with the residents" rather than "engage in point scoring".Philp added: "Zia, read the room, listen to the people clapping and read the room."Yusuf countered that it was "important that we hold everybody accountable for this situation" and said Philp had been "heavily involved in immigration and borders policy" for the Conservatives in government.Philp repeated his "read the room" suggestion, adding: "The public here want you to pipe down on the cheap politics."Yusuf dismissed the suggestion that he was engaging in "cheap politics" and repeated his criticism of the Conservatives' record, saying they "refused" to secure the country's borders when in power.As Yusuf spoke, Philp could be heard saying: "Buddy, I'm not here to give you comms advice, mate, you're in a hole stop digging."Philp told Yusuf he should "calm down", with the Reform politician repeating his request for the Conservative MP to "apologise to the British people".McNally thanked the pair for attending the press conference, adding: "I understand this is a passionate discussion and I respect you both for what you've got to do and what you represent."While the two parties are on the right of politics, it is unusual for them to share a platform to campaign and both are keen to stress their differences to voters.Reform leader Nigel Farage has pitched the party as replacing the "old, fuddy-duddy" Conservatives, and Tory leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would rather have another general election than do a deal with Reform to secure power.Government ministers want to use former military bases as part of efforts close all asylum hotels. Insisting that the MoD Bicester accommodation will be safe, the prime minister's deputy spokeswoman said such sites are "designed to be self-contained with 24/7 security and CCTV to minimise the impact on the local community".Prime Minister Andy Burnham has also previously said it should not just be the poorest communities receiving dispersed refugees and asylum seekers.Liberal Democrat MP Calum Miller told the BBC he was "very disappointed" but not "surprised" by the government's decision to grant planning permission.Miller, whose constituency of Bicester and Woodstock includes the military site, said "the government was marking the government's application".He said the decision "lays bare the weakness of the application and the many, many problems with it, because this is not a suitable site and it is not the right place to put a large-scale asylum centre".

schema.headline: Reform and Tory spokesmen in angry clash over immigration at Piddington

title: Microsoft 'deeply sorry' for global outage after almost 24 hours of disruption
description: Microsoft has said it is "deeply sorry" for the service outage to its products, including Outlook and Teams, which has caused disruption around the wo
body: Microsoft has said it is "deeply sorry" for the service outage to its products, including Outlook and Teams, which has caused disruption around the world.Services were broadly recovering by Friday afternoon, nearly 24 hours after issues began. Microsoft said it was making "encouraging progress", but added it does not know when services will fully recover.The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide.Microsoft said it was a technical issue introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and not related to cyber or artificial intelligence agents.Experts said the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of big tech providers.Users began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday.By Friday, the far-reaching issue was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, and trains, hospitals and courts in North America.In the UK, some parts of the NHS, including GPs and hospitals, were affected, as were some schools and police forces.UK cyber minister Liz Lloyd said the incident had "limited" impact on critical frontline services such as 999 calls, and there had been no disruption to the transport network.In Canada, however, the national rail network said passengers may not be able to receive email updates about their trips, and hospitals across the country also had issues with emails.In the US, staff members from the House of Representatives told Politico it had set back an entire day of legislative work as everything was on Microsoft's Outlook.Singapore's government acknowledged some of its systems had been impacted, and in India, the outage disrupted work for many on Friday.In Turkey, advisers and officials attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya were left frustrated by being unable to access Outlook.The issues also affected smaller businesses and individuals.Microsoft first acknowledged users in the Americas were unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes at 17:54 GMT on Thursday, and shortly after warned the disruption was possibly affecting Microsoft 365 globally.While it launched an investigation and engineers began working to restore services, by 04:36 on Friday Microsoft was reporting only a "partial recovery" in some parts of the world.By 13:32, the tech giant said there were "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" across much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in the Asia Pacific region.Microsoft said it restored services gradually due to the scale of the problem and to help ensure services remain stable once they are up and running again."We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," a Microsoft spokesperson said."We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously."Microsoft said it has no "ETA" for when services will be fully recovered.A full post-incident report will be released once Microsoft has completed a review.Experts said while workers may have been happy to not have email access for the day, the incident showed the dependence many organisations have on these cloud-based services."The global Microsoft outage is a stark reminder of how heavily we rely on a handful of big tech providers," said Rob Demain, chief executive of cybersecurity firm e2e-assure.Matt Saunders, field chief technology officer at tech consultancy Adaptavist, said it would be challenging to mitigate against a similar problem."Classic IT disaster planning strategies suggest using a second service for resilience, but in practice, it's almost impossible for a business to function without tools such as Microsoft," he said."In the wake of this outage, organisations must have a plan in place for how to work without such tools, for when incidents like this occur."

schema.headline: Microsoft 'deeply sorry' for global outage after almost 24 hours of disruption

title: Former Hamas bodyguard guilty of Birmingham knife attack
description: Image source, West Midlands PoliceImage caption, Mohammed Alfatih was granted asylum in the UK in 2015 and British citizenship in 2020ByPhil MackieRep
body: Image source, West Midlands PoliceImage caption, Mohammed Alfatih was granted asylum in the UK in 2015 and British citizenship in 2020ByPhil MackieReporting fromat Birmingham Crown CourtDaniel SandfordHome Affairs correspondent and Rushdi Abu AloufGaza correspondentUpdated 5 hours agoA former Hamas bodyguard, wanted in Germany over an alleged plot to murder Jewish people, has been found guilty of a knife attack on a bailiff outside his UK home.Mohammed Alfatih, previously known as Mohammed Naim, was regularly seen acting as a bodyguard for a former leader of Hamas in 2006. He was granted asylum in the UK in 2015 and British citizenship in 2021.The 40-year-old was found guilty by majority verdict of unlawfully wounding a bailiff who had come to repossess his wife's car, possession of two knives and criminal damage. He was cleared of wounding with intent.Alfatih was under surveillance by a counter-terror unit at the moment he attacked the bailiff in Birmingham last year. The son of a senior Hamas official, he could not be named during his trial due to reporting restrictions.During the trial, footage was shown of Alfatih brandishing two large kitchen knives outside his home in the suburb of Kings Heath and trying to stab the bailiff as he drove away.He told the court he chased the victim across the street to scare him away after his wife was asked to settle her debts of more than £2,250 linked to unpaid parking fines. Her car had been clamped by the enforcement officer, who was involved in a struggle inside Alfatih's terraced home.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Alfatih, circled, was bodyguard for Ismail Haniyeh before being removed from his postJurors were not told of Alfatih's links to proscribed terrorist group Hamas or his work as a bodyguard to its now-deceased former leader Ismail Haniyeh.But it can now be revealed that while detained for the attack in Birmingham, he was re-arrested when authorities in Germany said he had been part of an alleged gun plot to attack Jewish targets there.It is alleged Alfatih was an organiser and was involved in the movement of weapons. German authorities also allege he had pre-recorded a video wearing a balaclava and sunglasses claiming the attack was planned on behalf of the Izzedine al-Qassam Brigades, the military wing of Hamas. The alleged attack was prevented after a tip-off from the Israeli intelligence agency Mossad.Alfatih, who was born in Germany, is expected to be extradited to the country after he has served his sentence in the UK.Image source, West Midlands PoliceImage caption, Alfatih faces sentencing in Birmingham on 11 JanuaryDuring his evidence, Alfatih did not mention Hamas but told the court he had been tortured for 25 days while detained in Egypt in 2010.The father-of-four, an IT worker, failed in a legal application to try to get the wounding charges thrown out on the grounds of prejudicial media coverage about the investigation in Germany. During the two-week trial at Birmingham Crown Court, the jury was shown video footage of Alfatih lashing out with a knife at the broken window of a van on 14 October last year.Bailiff Kevin Bucknall was left with cuts to his head and required hospital treatment, but the defendant had pleaded not guilty on the grounds of self-defence.Alfatih told jurors it had happened a day after he had learned one of his brothers had been killed in Gaza. He also said while giving evidence that traumatic experiences in his past included being shot and injured on two different occasions.Image source, Der SpiegelImage caption, German prosecutors have named Alfatih in relation to extradition proceedings"I just want to be as honest as I can," he told the jury. "I don't think I was even in my full mind. I didn't intend anything other than him moving away."I wasn't anything more than terrified."Defence barrister Kate O'Raghallaigh said Alfatih had a heightened perception of danger, triggered by fear and desperation he had previously experienced.Jurors deliberated for more than six hours over three days before convicting him, with Alfatih heard mumbling to himself as the verdicts were returned. He has been in custody since the knife attack and now faces sentencing in Birmingham on 11 January, as well as separate extradition proceedings at Westminster Magistrates' Court.Image source, SuppliedImage caption, Jurors were not told of Alfatih's links to proscribed terrorist group HamasThe BBC understands that when Alfatih went by the name of Naim, he enrolled in a VIP protection course and was selected to accompany Haniyeh on trips to Egypt and other countries between 2006 and 2008. However, he was later removed from the role due to his behaviour.The second son of former Hamas health minister Bassem Naim, he later spent time in Malaysia, Qatar and Turkey before arriving in Britain. Following his conviction, a government source said it was "staggering" that he was granted asylum and later given citizenship. A Home Office spokesperson added Hamas was a proscribed terrorist organisation and the government condemned "those who choose to support its activities and further its aims".Additional reporting by Josh SandifordGet in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Birmingham and the Black Country

schema.headline: Former Hamas bodyguard guilty of Birmingham knife attack

title: Owain Wyn Evans completes Children in Need bike ride in Cardiff
description: Presenter Owain Wyn Evans has completed his challenge of cycling through all four UK nations to raise money for BBC Children in Need.The Welsh host of
body: Presenter Owain Wyn Evans has completed his challenge of cycling through all four UK nations to raise money for BBC Children in Need.The Welsh host of BBC Radio 2's Early Breakfast Show rode almost 400 miles, setting off from Glasgow and finishing in Cardiff on Friday.The challenge started on 9 November in Scotland and over the next five days, Owain rode through Northern Ireland, England and Wales and raised £3,853,530 in the process.Reflecting on his journey, he said: "This has been the hardest challenge of my life, 100%."I can't believe I'm here. It's overwhelming, all the love and passion and commitment people have shown."The BBC said Owain's challenge would be the "greatest-ever distance" covered in a Radio 2 endeavour for the charity.He crossed the finish line in Cardiff's Central Square  just after 11:00 GMT, and was greeted by a crowd cheering him on before he was met by his husband, Arran Rees.Owain, 42, whose bike was named Shania Chain, and decked out in Children in Need colours - Pudsey's favourite yellow with coloured spots - said: "Thank you so much everyone, from me and Shania."Honestly, this has felt so far away for such a long time. I can't believe that I'm here with this welcome and the sun's out."Hollywood actor Luke Evans announced the route to Owain each day on BBC Radio 2.During the 640km feat, he was also surprised with the premiere of Steps' brand-new version of their debut hit 5, 6, 7, 8, retitled 5, 6, 7, donate, which featured new lyrics and extra vocals.It was recorded to help boost Owain's spirits on the longest day of his challenge.The broadcaster also expressed his gratitude for the support of Radio 2 listeners.His messages of support from public figures included one from the Princess of Wales, who recorded a message for him in Welsh, saying: "Hi Owain, it's Catherine, you're doing so well. Keep going. Wishing you all the very best."Shania Twain was so impressed that the bike had been named after her that she sent a message of good luck before the challenge.She said: "Hi Owain, Shania Twain here. You're about to take on an incredible challenge for BBC Children in Need, cycling 400 miles through all four nations."As you set off in Glasgow, I just want to say: 'Let's Go, Owain!' We'll be cheering you on all the way. Good luck."She sent him another message when he finished, saying: "Congratulations on completing your incredible challenge for Children in Need. You're still the one my friend, sending you all my love."Helen Thomas, head of Radio 2, said: "Owain truly captured the hearts of the nation this week as he battled through his epic four nations Challenge."On behalf of all the Radio 2 listeners as well as the thousands of children and families who will benefit from his Herculean fundraising efforts we simply can't thank him enough. Diolch Owain! "

schema.headline: Owain Wyn Evans completes Children in Need bike ride in Cardiff

title: Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine
description: Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine.That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of
body: Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine.That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of Russia's neighbour nearly five years ago and who continues to reject the idea of a comprehensive ceasefire.And what, in Moscow's view, is a prerequisite for peace?The Kremlin spelt it out after talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner: "A new, long-term architecture of indivisible security and peace."Translated from Kremlin-speak, it means Moscow wants to change the security set-up of Europe in a way that benefits Russia.What Russia is pushing for is, potentially, the biggest change to European security arrangements since the end of the Cold War.The Kremlin has put back on the table its controversial proposal from December 2021 – the "draft treaties" with the US and Nato which would not only have put the brakes on the alliance's eastward enlargement by giving Moscow cast-iron guarantees that, for instance, Ukraine and Georgia would never be allowed to join, but also rolled back Nato military infrastructure from countries of central and eastern Europe which became Nato members following the dissolution of the Soviet Union.Western leaders dismissed such demands as an unacceptable Russian ultimatum. Two months later Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.The "draft treaties" were put away. Now they are out of the geopolitical filing cabinet, and being quoted again by the Kremlin.What is more, Yuri Ushakov, Putin's foreign policy aide, has suggested that Moscow is about to "add certain new considerations" to its list of demands in light of Western efforts "to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia".That does not mean, of course, that Western governments will accept them.But the fact that the question of European security is featuring now in discussions on Ukraine is viewed here as a victory for Moscow."In December 2021 Russia actively proposed that Nato rethink the security system in Europe," wrote newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda earlier this week."Our proposals were almost laughed at."Having secured one victory by forcing the West to think about security, our diplomats need a second by making the West heed Russia's concerns about Nato enlargement."The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, has called Russia's demands for a new European security architecture a "trap" designed to "shift attention away from a ceasefire"."The sequencing of Ukraine-Russia talks is important," Kallas wrote on social media. "The priority should be securing a ceasefire, followed by a peace agreement. Only then can there be discussions on Europe's wider security architecture."Europe's problem is that, right now, it is not at the table.Moscow has had no desire to give it a chair. It has slammed European leaders for their military support for Kyiv and tough stance on Russia.This week's peace talks in Abu Dhabi involved Ukraine, Russia and the US.After his discussions in Moscow, Witkoff indicated that Putin had agreed to the idea of European representatives joining the next round of Ukraine peace talks.But on Friday the Kremlin indicated a final decision on European participation had not been taken."Once we understand their true intentions and their readiness to facilitate the peace process, then it will be possible to take a decision about dialogue on Ukraine in a wider format," said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.And what of Putin?At the talks with Witkoff and Kushner he was sounding uncompromising and confident.You can see why.The Americans are knocking at his door and seeking a deal and the Europeans are contemplating contacts with him. Last month the leaders of Norway and Finland reached out and called him.And next week in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, Putin may have a separate meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. Russian media are already comparing them to the "Big Three" - Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill - who met in 1945 to reorganise post-World War Two Europe.And yet, after nearly five years of war, Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.The Russian economy is under increasing pressure.Ukrainian drone strikes continue to target Russian oil refineries, sparking fears of new fuel shortages.But, so far, none of this has convinced the Kremlin leader to end the fighting.

schema.headline: Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine

title: Police investigating David Walliams over reports alleging serious sexual offences
description: The Metropolitan Police has launched an investigation into David Walliams over reports of "alleged serious sexual offences".It comes after ITV News an
body: The Metropolitan Police has launched an investigation into David Walliams over reports of "alleged serious sexual offences".It comes after ITV News and the Guardian published reports alleging that Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women.The Met said that the allegations being investigated are separate from those reported by ITV and the Guardian, but as "part of their investigation, detectives are also proactively reviewing that reporting to establish whether there is any evidence of offences".When those allegations were first reported, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".In a statement released on Friday, the Met said it had "received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving a man now in his 50s"."Those who have come forward are being supported by specialist officers," the statement added.Detective Superintendent Mike Cagney said: "We would encourage anyone who has been the victim of a sexual offence to come forward and speak to us, no matter when it happened."We know reporting allegations of this nature can be daunting, but specialist officers are on hand to provide support, answer questions and guide you through the process."Allegations against the entertainer and children's author were published after he lost a legal bid to stop claims against him being made public by the media.Some of the women in the investigation accused Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers. One now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault". Walliams strongly denied he had any sexual contact with the girl.He said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and that he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.The Guardian and ITV News said that several of the women, who do not know one another, allege they were targets of unwanted sexual advances from Walliams.The investigation also claimed Walliams had a sexual relationship with at least one junior employee at publisher HarperCollins, and pursued another.Other women alleged inappropriate behaviour at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room.In a letter addressed to journalists working on the ITV and Guardian investigation, Walliams wrote: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with."I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. "And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."Walliams shot to fame in the early 2000s with BBC sketch comedy Little Britain, served as a judge on ITV's Britain's Got Talent and launched a best-selling series of children's books.

schema.headline: Police investigating David Walliams over reports alleging serious sexual offences

title: Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost?
description: Some Microsoft 365 services have been affected by "connectivity problems" with problems reported in at least 74 countries.From late on Thursday, custo
body: Some Microsoft 365 services have been affected by "connectivity problems" with problems reported in at least 74 countries.From late on Thursday, customers reported varying levels of access - many were unable to send or receive emails, view certain files or details on their calendar apps. But some users were able to use Teams, messaging and online meeting functions without issues. As of Friday afternoon, Microsoft said it had seen "encouraging recovery progress" in Europe and improvement in North America.The company added that it was focused on "addressing the remaining areas of disruption" but warned "some users may still experience intermittent issues".In a later statement, the company said it was continuing to see improvements "with email queues significantly reduced and approaching normal levels".The company attributed the ongoing outage to an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade."We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions," it said on Friday.Although email service Outlook appears to be resuming, the outage has so far lasted for more than 20 hours - in outage terms that is considered a long time.Prof James Ferryman from the University of Reading's department of computer science said the details the company has disclosed provide some clues."What Microsoft has told us is that the part of its servers that sets up secure connections is getting swamped, and once that happens the server just stops answering," he said."The trouble is that this kind of failure snowballs."One server falls over, its work gets passed to the next one, and meanwhile huge numbers of phones and laptops keep trying to get back in."You can't just turn it all back on at once. You have to bring it back bit by bit."The challenge is therefore not just fixing the fault, but managing the huge surge of devices trying to reconnect once services start coming back online.Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies including Skype and Uber, said this could be the "most disruptive" business email outage "of all time".He said it was still difficult to know just how many people have been affected by the disruption, but added he "cannot recall" an outage over business email ever taking this long to return to normal.Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt told the BBC the outage could have far-reaching consequences."Microsoft is a massive part of the internet backbone and reminds us how critical email still is. "Not only does this outage affect many people's ability to work but also things like the ability to communicate about appointments, purchase things that need verification, create or access accounts and services," he said.In a statement, Microsoft said it was "deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. "We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services."More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website. The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed.Microsoft 365 is used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services.Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic both earlier reported problems as a result of the outage.ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which had caused some tools to not work as expected.From city governments in the US to Australian spy agencies, disruption across the globe has been widespread.Courts from Los Angeles to Texas earlier warned that communications might be delayed.In Canada, the public broadcaster CBC reported that a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto was experiencing email issues, but that patient care was not affected.The government of Japan also said its shared IT platform had been disrupted.Across the UK, GP surgeries, pharmacies, police and schools have been affected by the outage.Some GP surgeries had urged patients not to submit messages via their website while police forces were also earlier asking the public to call if they want to make a report.Additional reporting by Henry Moore

schema.headline: Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost?

title: Pope Leo visits the Peruvian city that has embraced him as one of its own
description: Image source, Reuters / Pilar OlivaresImage caption, The Pope, who has Peruvian citizenship, lived in Chiclayo for several yearsByJosé Carlos CuetoBBC
body: Image source, Reuters / Pilar OlivaresImage caption, The Pope, who has Peruvian citizenship, lived in Chiclayo for several yearsByJosé Carlos CuetoBBC News Mundo in Chiclayo, PeruPope Leo XIV has celebrated Mass near the Peruvian city where he made his name as a compassionate bishop who worked closely with poor and migrant communities.The ceremony was held on Friday at a park in Pimentel, about 10km (six miles) from Chiclayo in northern Peru as part of his tour of Latin America. The Vatican estimates more than 1.5 million people gathered to welcome the pontiff."Thank you for your affection, support and prayers," the Pope told followers. "Especially for my health during this time of trial which, with God's help, I am overcoming," he added, referencing the surgery he had for lung cancer which took place just weeks ago. Some of the crowd arrived 12 hours in advance to wait in vigil before the Mass began. "We spent the night praying, alongside family, excited to welcome the Pope from Chiclayo," said Isa Orderique. Image source, Tiziana FABI / AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Pope Leo celebrated Mass in front of a jubilant crowdMany came from across Peru and even neighbouring countries to attend.Merli Cruz Guerrero, from an area near the Ecuadorean border, travelled several hours by bus to attend. She also spent the entire night waiting.Of all the events the Pope has attended so far during his visit to Peru, this felt particularly emotional. The crowd fell into a hushed silence as the pontiff's motorcade approached. They waited eagerly for his arrival despite spending long hours out in the open with the temperature pushing past 30C. For many living here, the fact that the Pope worked extensively in this region before becoming the head of the Catholic Church has put them in the spotlight."The Pope has come home and Chiclayo is celebrating," said Lisbeth Díaz, a teacher who worked with Pope Leo when he served as the city's bishop between 2015 and 2023.Image caption, Lisbeth Díaz says Chiclayo is celebrating the Pope's returnPeru is the longest stop on the first tour of Latin America by the pontiff, who was elected in May 2025.The trip has also taken in Argentina and Uruguay, but his time in this country carries particular significance.The Pope not only lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023 but also became a citizen of the country in 2015, forging close ties with local communities.Around Chiclayo, it is hard to meet anyone who doesn't claim to be a friend of the Pope or have a special anecdote about him.Some recall how he would enjoy sampling Peruvian delicacies at El Trébol, a restaurant next to the city's cathedral. Others remember his love of tennis.But for many it's the more serious moments of his time here, such as helping launch soup kitchens during the Covid-19 pandemic, or wading through deep waters on horseback when floods hit the area.Several of these images are on display in a small museum dedicated to him at the entrance to the bishop's residence.Image caption, Commemorative pictures of the Pope are sold in the main of square of Chiclayo, including a famous image of him visiting a remote village on horsebackBut for the city, and for a country that calls him the "Peruvian Pope", his return home means much more than a collection of photographs and anecdotes."It is the return of the man who brought Peruvians closer to the Church," said Samuel David Miranda Atoche, a local parish priest from Chiclayo who was ordained by the Pope back when he was still the bishop and known under his birth name of Robert Prevost.And it is not just local people he connected with, according to Díaz, who came to Chiclayo from Venezuela."It was difficult for him to see so many migrants living on the streets," she added, recalling the time when large numbers of Venezuelans came through Chiclayo escaping the political and economic crisis in their home country."So, he got in touch with the migration authorities and coordinated with other organisations to speed up the paperwork needed for many of us to obtain legal residency and work permits."Robert Prevost's time here as bishop also involved difficult decisions, such as having to deal with the controversy and scandal surrounding the dissolution of Sodalitium of Christian Life, a Peruvian Catholic organisation that had faced decades of sexual abuse allegations.Santiago Roncagliolo, a Peruvian writer and journalist who has studied the Pope's life, believes his handling of that crisis earned him the favour of his predecessor, Pope Francis, and helped set him on the path to the papacy.Father Miranda also stressed the role the now-pontiff played in bringing people together."If there is one thing Bishop Prevost worked for here," he added, referring to the Pope by his previous title, "it was unity".That unity has been on display in the run up to the Mass, with the square in front of Chiclayo Cathedral filled with joyous celebrations for days.Image caption, Father Samuel David Miranda Atoche says the Pope brought Peruvians closer to the ChurchNormally, 800,000 people live in the city and its surrounding area, but estimates say the Pope's visit has caused that to double.Local businesses have been capitalising on the Pope's popularity to boost sales and hotels have sharply increased their nightly room rates.But that didn't seem to put off the faithful who gathered for the Mass. Shouts of: "The Pope is from Chiclayo!" echoed across the field during the event. Their affection was clearly reflected by the pontiff."As I look at your faces, a prayer of thanksgiving to the Lord arises in my heart," he said from the stage, "for the blessing you have been and continue to be in my life."

title: Conservative Party pays artist for Burnham images after legal threat
description: The Conservatives have agreed to pay an artist who threatened to sue the party after it used his illustration of Andy Burnham to mock the prime minist
body: The Conservatives have agreed to pay an artist who threatened to sue the party after it used his illustration of Andy Burnham to mock the prime minister.Stanley Chow posted on Facebook that the party had used the picture - which Burnham has used on social media - without permission.He had sought legal advice and threatened to take action against the party. It is understood the Tories agreed to pay a £1,000 fee for use of the image - and contributed an unknown sum to Chow's legal fees.The Conservatives had distributed water bottles with the image on them - accusing Burnham of being a "bottler".Chow posted on Facebook: "The Conservative Party have settled after their recent indiscretion of using my image without my permission."He added: "Maybe ask first… admittedly I would have said no, but it would have been a damn sight cheaper for the Tory Party if they just hired any illustrator to do their take on a cartoon of Burnham… hopefully this a lesson learned. Copyright matters."A Conservative spokesman said: "The Conservative Party values the importance of intellectual property in the creative industries. We consider this matter closed."

schema.headline: Conservative Party pays artist for Burnham images after legal threat

title: Man jailed for grooming 70 girls on Snapchat, Wink and Roblox
description: A man who groomed at least 70 girls and manipulated them into sending sexually explicit videos and images of themselves has been sentenced to 30 years
body: A man who groomed at least 70 girls and manipulated them into sending sexually explicit videos and images of themselves has been sentenced to 30 years in prison. Bilal Kazi, 27, targeted his victims - aged between 10 and 17 - using apps including Snapchat, Wink and Roblox between August 2021 and August 2025.Kazi, a student from India who was studying at the University of Chester, posed as a 14-year-old white British teenage boy and made his victims believe they were in a relationship with him.He was jailed after pleading guilty to 37 charges including making indecent images, blackmail and inciting a child to engage in sexual activity.Warning: This article contains distressing informationKazi must serve a minimum of 20 years in prison before being eligible for parole and will be on the sex offenders register for life.Once eligible for parole he will be on licence for eight years.In a personal impact statement read out at Chester Crown Court earlier, one victim said she had struggled with anxiety as Kazi, who later moved to Birmingham, had "taken away a sense of privacy and security"."I am doing my best to move forward but the effects are still with me," she said."The harm caused is not limited to the time events took place - they continue to affect my daily life."The court heard that some of the victims had attempted suicide, struggled with anxiety and developed eating disorders.One victim, who was 13 years old when Kazi first contacted her, said he took her "innocence away"."I hope one day I can get on with my life," she said. Judge Stephen Everett said Kazi was a sexual predator who took advantage of "what appears to be a lack of proper security on social media sites"."It is incomprehensible to me why any person would do what you did to those little girls," the court heard."This was bad enough, but when one learns of all the other images you demanded for your deviant sexual desires, we will never know how many victims there were."Children who believed they were safe in their own homes - and by your gross misuse of social media  - you took away all of that safety, all of that comfort."The judge said it was difficult to find any mitigating factors and said he doubted Kazi's remorse."You are a very dangerous person," he said."In a sophisticated way, you got into the minds of young people and got them to do things that were totally alien to them."Talking about one victim, Everett said: "She won't look back on her childhood with any great pleasure - she will look on it totally blighted at what this fiend did to her."He added: "These are not just pictures on a computer these are young lives that have been blighted."Det Con Georgia Hughes, from Cheshire Police, said Kazi had not shown any remorse."The girls targeted by Kazi were young and vulnerable," she said. "For many, their interactions with him were their first experience of what they believed to be a romantic relationship."Exploiting that trust, Kazi manipulated them into believing that his behaviour was normal."Many lived in constant fear of what he would do if they failed to comply with his demands, and some have carried that fear with them for years. "What should have been important formative years have instead been overshadowed by the trauma of Kazi's abuse."Speaking on online safety, Sgt Ross Peel said the force's message to parents was to "speak to your children and take an interest in the apps and platforms they are using". "The potential for online offending is vast," he said."And offenders can target children from anywhere in the world."By educating yourselves and your children about online safety and the risks associated with communicating with people they do not know online, you can help protect them."

title: How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House
description: How close is Donald Trump to Jensen Huang?The answer is very.The Nvidia boss was one of the few business leaders with direct access to the US presiden
body: How close is Donald Trump to Jensen Huang?The answer is very.The Nvidia boss was one of the few business leaders with direct access to the US president. He had met Trump repeatedly, travelled with him to Britain and, in May, joined him on Air Force One for his trip to China.Jensen Huang wasn't just another tech billionaire seeking the president's ear. He had become an important voice in one of the biggest arguments inside the administration: how much of America's most advanced technology should be allowed to reach China.Nvidia makes the chips that power the AI revolution. Washington has restricted exports of its most advanced processors to China since 2022, believing they could help Beijing develop its military and technological capabilities.But enforcing those restrictions is difficult. Chips can be bought legally by customers in countries such as Singapore and Malaysia and then diverted to China. Chinese companies can also rent access to computing power through data centres outside the country.Jensen Huang has long argued that the restrictions are counterproductive. They shut Nvidia out of a huge market and encourage Chinese companies to develop their own alternatives. Trump appeared sympathetic to this view, allowing Nvidia to resume sales of certain chips to China last year in return for a share of the revenue, although its most advanced Blackwell chips remain off limits.But that relationship now looks rather more complicated.The allegations surrounding Jensen Huang's reported affair with Alice Huang, of no relation but a former executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed, have raised the possibility that a foreign intelligence operation was targeting not just a powerful businessman, but someone with unusually close access to the American president. US intelligence reportedly suspects Alice Huang of having links to Chinese intelligence. Beijing has rejected the allegations. Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. But the affair has opened up a much bigger question: what did the administration in Washington know, and what did it do about it?That question leads directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.His department was responsible for controlling exports of sensitive American technology. It was also being pressed to act on concerns about Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. On Thursday, Megaspeed chief executive, Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan, said the company "takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously" and is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government". He said the company had co-operated with US Commerce Department inspections.A highly classified memo was shared with Lutnick about the concerns surrounding Alice Huang and Megaspeed. He resisted taking action against the company, a decision that is now under scrutiny. Other senior officials wanted a tougher response. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was among those who reportedly questioned why Megaspeed had not been placed on the Commerce Department's blacklist.On Friday, Bessent pointed the finger at Commerce for not blacklisting the company, telling CNBC that several government agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months"."But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added.There have also been questions about why an investigation into the Singapore-based company was stopped after Nvidia intervened. The New York Times reported that Nvidia's general counsel contacted Commerce Department investigators probing suspected chip smuggling by Megaspeed invoking a senior Trump appointee. The department allegedly then froze its investigation and handed the case to the Justice Department.This apparently highlighted a significant disagreement about the direction of Trump's China policy. Huang wanted access to the Chinese market. Other officials were supposedly worried about the national security consequences. Lutnick was caught in the middle.Now the political pressure is building.Members of Congress from both parties want answers. Democrats have launched an investigation into how the Commerce Department vetted Chinese companies approved to buy AI chips. Republicans are also questioning the administration's approach.And Jensen Huang's departure has not eased the pressure.Republican representative John Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, said it was in the national interest for Nvidia and other American AI firms to succeed, but that companies "should never jeopardise our nation's security" by giving Chinese firms access to their most advanced chips.Senator Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said Huang's resignation did not absolve him of responsibility, and urged Lutnick to explain why export control loopholes remain open.Meanwhile Jensen Huang's team told Republican lawmakers on Wednesday that he plans to cooperate with their request to testify behind closed doors.The White House has not responded to the BBC's request for comment.It has, however, told the New York Post that Trump has complete confidence in Lutnick, describing him as "the most transformative commerce secretary in modern history".That is a fairly emphatic show of support, particularly amid reports that officials are weighing whether Lutnick should be forced out.There are some obvious questions. If Lutnick had indeed been warned about the risks, why did his department fail to act? And if other senior officials were indeed pressing for action, why did it take so long?The BBC has contacted the Commerce Department for comment. But there is an even bigger question for Trump.The president cultivated a close relationship with Huang. He was directly involved in decisions about chip sales to China. And, according to reporting in the New York Times, he was briefed on the intelligence concerns.This is becoming difficult to dismiss as the misjudgement of one businessman or one government department.Jensen Huang's personal life may have triggered the crisis, but the questions now reach into the White House itself. How much influence did he have? What did the president know? And who was ultimately responsible for protecting America's most sensitive technology?

title: Microsoft outage 'stark reminder' of how much we rely on tech
description: A critical Microsoft outage lasting more than 22 hours has raised questions about how heavily vital services rely on a handful of major tech firms.The
body: A critical Microsoft outage lasting more than 22 hours has raised questions about how heavily vital services rely on a handful of major tech firms.The disruption, which affected Microsoft 365 services such as Outlook, was caused by routine automated checks that took some servers offline, overloading the remaining ones with traffic.The recovery took nearly a full day while engineers gradually restored services, highlighting how embedded the tech giant's services are in modern society.Flora Hamilton, executive director of the Small Business Charter, said the outage was a "stark reminder" of how much firms "rely on digital systems" - like Microsoft Outlook - "to keep their operations running"."For many small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), access to email is fundamental to everything from communicating with customers and suppliers to generating income," she said.The disruption was not just confined to businesses, but also affected organisations and public institutions around the world.Around 430 million people globally use Microsoft 365, and issues were reported across more than 70 countries.The fallout from the outage had a wide-ranging effect, knocking out email systems for the US House of Representatives and Australian intelligence agencies, as well as disrupting court systems in Singapore and airline support desks in India.Microsoft has since apologised for the issue, which it said was due to a technical failure rather than a cyber-attack. There was no "ETA" for when services will be fully recovered, Microsoft added in a statement late on Friday (GMT).Walter Pasquarelli, an AI strategist, told the BBC that for governments, businesses and critical infrastructure, the outage had "put their vulnerabilities and dependence in plain sight"."Looking ahead, as AI assistants are plugged into our email, calendars and files, a failure like this may spread even further," he said.Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies, said while these kinds of outages weren't unheard of, what was unusual was the time it took for Microsoft to recover from it.A spokesperson for the US tech company said "given the scale of demand" it restored services gradually."While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration," a spokesperson said.Orosz said the resulting upset showed "our reliance on a few large US corporations".He said a solution for the future could be to split services per region to reduce the impact, something which already happens with Amazon's cloud computing service, AWS.For now, Microsoft said it was reviewing what went wrong, with the findings expected to inform steps to prevent a similar disruption from happening again.

schema.headline: Microsoft outage 'stark reminder' of how much we rely on tech

title: Pectus excavatum: 'My deformity left me feeling invisible'
description: My physical deformity left me feeling invisible - but one surgeon saw meImage caption, Charlie kept her condition hidden for years and says it made he
body: My physical deformity left me feeling invisible - but one surgeon saw meImage caption, Charlie kept her condition hidden for years and says it made her life "hell" at timesByHealth correspondent, BBC News NIAs a teenager at school, Charlie Clarke "felt awful" in her uniform, with a physical deformity leaving her so self-conscious that she hid from her classmates.At home, she wrapped her dressing gown tight around her chest, hoping it would conceal her condition - and didn't even tell her parents about it.Now 26, Charlie has lived with pectus excavatum - a congenital chest wall condition that can make the chest appear sunken or hollow - for years.As she awaits surgical treatment, she said the emotional and physical effects of the condition were "unimaginable and unignorable"."Having pectus excavatum, which is a disability and a deformity under my shirt, was at times hell," she said.Her worst memories from her teenage years are of hiding in the school bathroom during PE so other girls would not comment on her having "four breasts"."I got to a point where I felt awful wearing my school uniform because of how I looked, also because of how people looked at me and made comments about my chest," said Charlie, from County Down.Image source, Charlie ClarkeImage caption, Charlie didn't tell her parents about the severity of her condition for yearsThe condition, which affects one in every 200 people, means Charlie's heart and lungs are compressed, which triggers breathlessness and an increased heart rate that can cause her to lose consciousness.Charlie is one of 85 people in Northern Ireland who are waiting for surgery for pectus conditions.Many of them have been waiting for their operation for less than two years - but five have been on the list for longer than five years.The Department of Health said it acknowledged that some patients in Northern Ireland "have endured lengthy waits", adding that the volume of patients combined with "other demands on the thoracic surgery service have contributed to pressures on waiting times".But it said it had secured extra funding for more surgeries in order to reduce the amount of people on the waiting list, resulting in additional pectus procedures in the last three years.It also said it had agreed a further proposal "which should help to reduce both the number of patients waiting and the length of their waits". 'I was misdiagnosed'If diagnosed early, patients can often be treated without surgery.But getting that early diagnosis is key - and treatment depends on the type of pectus, how severe it is and the patient's age.Charlie said she was previously "misdiagnosed, including [being] told I had anxiety"."It wasn't until I had my shirt off in front of a clinical technician and she said they were unable to see my heart in a scan, it was compressed, and only then was I referred to a thoracic surgeon."That was when she was 23 years old, which is considered too old for non-surgical treatment.Image source, Charlie ClarkeImage caption, Charlie wants to raise awareness of the conditionA breakthrough came when Charlie met someone who truly understood her experience.Niall McGonigle, a Northern Ireland-based consultant thoracic surgeon, specialises in chest wall deformities.What makes his expertise particularly unique is that he suffered from a pectus deformity himself as a child and underwent surgery at 17."I was called freak and a mutant at school," he said."It drove me away from sports because of changing for PE - I was bullied."It is what started my interest in medicine... I was profoundly interested in surgery and specifically pectus."McGonigle said the condition was not recognised in Northern Ireland, and patients are often dismissed as asking for cosmetic surgery, which is not the case.Image source, Niall McGonigleImage caption, Niall McGonigle was inspired to become a surgeon after his experience with a pectus deformity"There is a lot of evidence to show there are restrictions on the lungs and heart, which can be debilitating," he said."If this is diagnosed early, patients can be treated with non-surgical services."But Northern Ireland doesn't provide this and our young people are having to go to England instead."McGonigle said Northern Ireland's limited pectus surgery service had been undermined by inconsistent funding.Charlie's surgery will involve two metal bars being placed in her chest and a metal plate in her sternum, allowing her heart and lungs to return to their natural positions.She said she was speaking out to raise awareness of the condition and to help others who have it, including her 11-year-old sister."I don't want her to have to wait this long and for her life to be paused and for her condition to become life-threatening," Charlie said.What is pectus excavatum?Pectus excavatum, also known as "funnel chest", is different for everyone. Most who have the condition were born with it.A patient's breastbone curves inwards, with a dip the ribs, which can leave the chest appearing sunken or hollow.It is usually more noticeable in childhood or teenage years.One treatment is vacuum bell therapy, using a suction device that sits over the sunken part of the chest to gradually lift the breastbone forwards.It works best in younger people with a flexible chest wall and a relatively shallow deformity.Another treatment, compression bracing, involves a specially fitted brace and is most effective in teenagers - but generally less so once the chest becomes rigid in adulthood.In its statement, the Department of Health said work it carried out in 2023 led to the commissioning of a service for "non-surgical bracing of pectus carinatum".It added it is understood this "can, in appropriately selected patients, negate the requirement for surgery"."The impact of this service will be evaluated, including its potential to free up theatre capacity for those conditions which can only be resolved surgically."Image caption, Vacuum bell therapy is a non-surgical treatment that works best for younger peopleLast month, patients and health professionals from across the UK met in Belfast to discuss the condition.Simon Kendall, of the charity Pectus Matters, said early treatment saves the health service money in the long term."If you get that treatment when the patient is young and chest wall is more flexible you can avoid the big operations in the future."

title: Formula 1's diamond 'heist': an unsolved mystery?
description: Where were you between the hours of 1pm and 3pm on 23 May 2004?If you were in Monaco, consider yourself a suspect - or at least a witness - in Formula
body: Where were you between the hours of 1pm and 3pm on 23 May 2004?If you were in Monaco, consider yourself a suspect - or at least a witness - in Formula 1's biggest unsolved mystery.A $300,000 diamond was last seen stuck to the front of an F1 car before it crashed on the first lap of the Grand Prix and it still has not been found 22 years later.Did someone pick it up? Was it swept up with all the debris? Did it slip down a drain? Was it even a real diamond?Someone, somewhere, knows something.The reason why a 1.4 carat diamond was attached to the most delicate part of a car that reaches 200mph in a race was straightforward: publicity.Jaguar Racing's results on the track had been mediocre at best since becoming an F1 team in 2000 and by 2004 its parent company Ford had decided it would be pulling them out of the sport."My job flipped from primarily running the team to primarily selling the team and finding a new owner or they would shut it down," former team principal Tony Purnell tells BBC Sport."It was probably the worst year of my life. Particularly because for the first few months I was sworn to secrecy."His team needed some good PR to divert attention away from performance and improve its appeal.They had enjoyed a successful promotional weekend in Silverstone the previous season thanks to a tie-up with Terminator 3 and so director of communications Nav Sidhu was looking to recreate the magic with another bit of help from a movie."I'd heard on the grapevine, around about the winter of 2003, that they were making Ocean's Twelve and we discovered that they were shooting some of the scenes in Monte Carlo," Sidhu says."One thing led to another and before you knew it, we had agreed [a deal] with George Clooney, Brad Pitt and Matt Damon."Sidhu had arranged with legendary Hollywood producer Jerry Weintraub to have the film's branding and stars take over the team for the Monaco weekend.The film plot centred on an audacious theft of a diamond-encrusted Faberge egg. Sidhu decided he wanted some sparkle on his cars too at the most glamorous race in the F1 calendar.Sidhu negotiated with diamond company Steinmetz that the two Jaguar cars would have gems - which would today be worth about $1m in total - attached to them.What happened next, though, was not part of the script.While the champagne corks were popping on nearby mega yachts in the principality, the diamonds were being hand-delivered into the garages. There were two that would be mounted on to the car and a larger gem just for the photos.The diamonds for the cars were encased by steel and fixed to the nose cones. One on experienced driver Mark Webber's car and one on rookie Christian Klien's.Webber was starting from 11th place in the grid and Klien - in only his sixth race - was starting from 14th. They weren't expected to challenge for the podium, but they were expected to bring the diamonds back.Monaco's street circuit is demanding, with narrow roads, tight turns and a tunnel.Overtaking is difficult and crashes are common - as Klien soon found out.In a chaotic first lap, the Austrian made contact with one of the Jordan cars exiting the Mirabeau corner. This damaged the front of his car - where the diamond was - and led to a slow collision with the barriers at the famous Loews hairpin.Klien climbed out unhurt but the front of the car was crumpled.It was not long before Sidhu had the diamond company on the phone asking if they would get their diamond back."I can't remember what I answered, but it certainly wasn't 'yes'," he says.He couldn't even get on to the track to have a look as the race had another 76 laps to go and only then would the car - which had been lifted off the track by a crane and left behind the barriers - return to the garage."I was consumed with getting to that spot as quickly as I possibly could," Sidhu says."That hour and a half waiting for the race to finish felt like a day and a half, every single lap was just like pulling teeth."By the time he had the chance to have a look, there was no sign of the diamond.But there were plenty of theories.Theory: it was not a real diamondSidhu completely denies the rumours of a fake diamond."I've learned that any diamond company is not going to go out there, particularly in the public domain, and use fake diamonds because clearly there's a high risk of being caught," he says."Had we used a fake diamond in that car and what took place took place, then clearly the embarrassment and the disrepute it would bring Jaguar, and Formula 1 for that matter, was too high risk."There's been loads of conspiracy theories about was it a real diamond or was Christian told to crash his car and I think that's what's given the story its life - there's a mystery to this story and that mystery will always breed different theories."Purnell backs up the legitimacy of the diamond, recalling a conversation he had with the managing director of the team, David Pitchforth."David said, 'Tony, it was definitely real because when they came to the office with it, I picked the diamond up, went to the window and scratched the window' because that's how to tell."Hearing that from Dave, I'm in no doubt it was the real thing that was put on the car."I don't know if one of our mechanics was switched on enough to make a fake, but I don't think so."Theory: someone pocketed it"I think somebody probably just picked it up, put it in their pocket and... they're probably smiling and thinking, 'it's in my drawer'," says Purnell."I do think also that a fairly large diamond zooming through at 100 miles an hour probably shattered. Somebody's got a little bit, somebody else has got another [little bit]."Maybe, sadly, just some guy was sweeping up the road or one of those trucks with the brushes and it all went down the sewer."It did occur to me that the ultimate thing would be if Clooney, Pitt and Damon had contrived to steal it because it was so in line with Ocean's Eleven. But that was a fantasy too far."There would have been hundreds, if not thousands, of people in the area because within an hour or so of the end of the race the circuit would have been returned to public roads.   Sidhu is pretty certain about what happened to the diamond: "Someone's picked it up."What people tend to do is, believe it or not, pick up bits of tyre rubber, you know, claim that as Michael Schumacher's front tyre rubber or whatever they can find."Somebody may have picked it up not having any idea it came off a car."There's a lot of diamonds in Monte Carlo. There's a lot of people walking around Monte Carlo with a lot of jewellery and a lot of stones."Somebody dropped a diamond in Monte Carlo. Well, they're not going to miss that, are they? Probably not."Theory: Klien crashed on purposeSidhu says the cost of the damage to the car was more than the cost of the diamond, which reports at the time said was uninsured.And points and a good result in the race were more valuable to the team and individuals than a diamond or the publicity a crash would bring. It was simply not worth crashing on purpose."For us, bringing two cars home, ideally in the points, had far bigger commercial benefits to us in terms of constructors' points, broadcast money, and more importantly, trying to retain our sponsors and trying to protect the integrity of the team," Sidhu explains.Klien drove straight into the barriers right in front of the marshals so would not have had the chance to start looking for a diamond or picking it up even if he had wanted to."Christian didn't try and say all the brakes failed or anything like that, he's just said 'I made a rookie mistake'," says Purnell."He was a young guy, first time, made a mistake, it happens. Doesn't usually happen with a $300,000 diamond flying into the crowd or wherever it went, but I'm sure Christian wasn't really aware of the diamond."No amount of money would have got Christian to do that [crash on purpose]. He wanted to make a success of what he was doing."While events were unfolding, Purnell had not really been thinking about the diamond. His main concern that day was that one of his drivers had crashed and the other also did not finish, and that this was not a good look in terms of pleasing current backers or attracting potential buyers."When Christian went into the wall and then later Mark retired, my entire thinking was 'Oh God. What am I going to say?' The chairman of HSBC [Jaguar's then sponsors] was there, Sir John Bond. Jackie [Stewart] was there."It was all about 'how am I going to explain another bad performance? How am I going to say 'just stick with the plan? We know what we're doing, it will take time' because sponsors don't have time. They want success."In the end, the missing diamond came to the rescue."No-one mentioned Jarno Trulli winning the Grand Prix, no-one asked how the Jaguars did. No-one was interested that Mark Webber's car broke as well. It was, 'where's the diamond?'" says Purnell."I remember talking to somebody in Detroit saying, 'fantastic publicity over here, you know we never hear anything about Formula 1 but it's on the newscasts, it's in the papers - fantastic'."Asked if the diamond mystery had helped the eventual sale of the team to Red Bull six months later, he replies: "I think that helped quite a lot because it buzzed the Jaguar team and showed that huge publicity was possible even if you weren't doing so well."Red Bull went on to become hugely successful, winning eight drivers' championships and six constructors' championships since joining F1."You couldn't design a better PR weekend," says Purnell.Even if it was not quite how it was planned and there is still the small matter of a missing diamond.
